Carte Blanche SHELL panel debate [6090]

By: Chwayitisa Futshane | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Protests, petitions and interdicts. They’re all good and well but in a country with an economy on its knees and mass unemployment - can we afford to reject possible solutions like gas exploration in

Unique Selling Point:
It's the environment versus the economy. In a gritty new-look segment - experts, activists and loud-mouths go head to head in a heated debate about whether the country should be putting the economy before the environment!

Summary:
One moderator, four voices and all in just seven minutes.

Further information:
At the beginning of December 2021, Impact Oil & Gas, an African exploration company, and BG International, a division of Royal Dutch Shell, won a case brought against them by the Border Deep Sea Angling Association, the Key Mouth Ski Boat Club, the NGO Natural Justice, and international activist group Greenpeace.

That case sought an urgent interdict against a seismic survey which had begun on 1 December, as per an exploration right first granted in 2014, and renewed twice thereafter, most recently in August 2021.

The applicants’ submissions in this regard, related to the detrimental impact of the seismic survey on the environment, and marine life in particular.

The oil and gas exploration companies had to return to the same court within days to defend against a different group of applicants seeking essentially the same thing: an interim interdict on proceeding with the seismic survey while the legality of their exploration right was brought before the court.

This time, a different judge, Judge Gerald Bloem, came to exactly the opposite conclusion, despite being faced with very similar facts.

The judgment found that the consultation process was ‘inadequate and substantially flawed’.

Meanwhile Mineral Resources and Energy Minister Gwede Mantashe has said that government will not change its stance on supporting the proposed seismic survey by Shell on the Eastern Cape’s Wild Coast.

The Minister also criticised locals for being used by environmentalists, who according to him, wanted to stifle development in the province.

Mantashe maintains that the Eastern Cape would remain underdeveloped if it did not use opportunities such as Shell’s seismic survey, which was meant to determine whether there was oil and gas off the Wild Coast.

Mantashe said it was a bad idea to block Shell’s project as the petroleum giant was being welcomed in other countries such as Namibia, to conduct the same seismic surveys. This meant that South Africa would potentially lose out on massive development and employment opportunities, he added.

This background brings us to the heart of the debate.

For the moment Shell have been ordered to put an end to its seismic surveys but should this this mean the end of gas exploration in the country as some environmentalists believe?

Not so fast it seems!

In the West Coast, Searcher GeoData, which provides subsurface exploration data, has been awarded a reconnaissance permit for a multi-client speculative 2D and/or 3D marine seismic programme to explore for oil and gas over vast areas of the ocean stretching from Cape Point to the Namibian border in an area known as the Orange Basin.

Its environmental management plan states the programme will potentially allow South Africa to “optimise its own indigenous resources to provide its identified oil and gas needs, rather than having to import, as at present”.

Are we placing the real needs of employment and economic growth in places like the Eastern Cape above the protection of the environment? And does science support the notion that seismic surveys will destroy the coastline?

Is it one or the other, or can it be both?

And if seismic surveys are here to stay, how then do we still protect the environment?

Let's debate!

Moderator - Bongani Bingwa

RICHARD SPOOR
Human rights lawyer and activist

ALDWORTH MBALATI
DNG ENERGY – founder and CEO

IAN COX
Attorney and commentator on Shell’s Seismic survey interdicts

SIFISO SKENJANA
Chief Economist, Executive Head: Research and Strategic Advisory at IQbusiness South Africa

Press Release:


The Environment Versus the Economy
It’s a simple enough question: can South Africa afford to place the environment before the economy? The answer is complex. Government says tapping into our proven natural gas reserves is necessary for economic growth, while conservationists argue our natural heritage must be protected at all costs. In a gritty new-look debate segment, a human rights activist, an economist, and a lawyer each fight their corner.
Producer: Chwayitisa Futshane | Moderator: Busisiwe Gumede-Chizhanje

Script:


PANEL DEBATE SCRIPT

Protests … petitions … and court interdicts…

Late last year, oil and gas giant, SHELL, was successfully prevented from undertaking its controversial seismic surveys off the Wild Coast.

It’s a complex and emotive issue that could potentially see SHELL’s vessel, blasting loud sound pulses at the ocean floor, as it searches for reserves of natural gas. But, while the legal battle continues, it’s generated debate on a broader question: Does South Africa have the luxury of choosing the environment over the economy?

I’m Busisiwe Gumede-Chi---zhan---je and you’re watching the first instalment of Carte Blanche Debates…


Fighting their corners tonight: …. He calls himself a conservationist with a deep affection for the Transkei… Attorney Ian Cox ….



Thought leader and Chief Economist at IQ Business, Sifiso Skhenjana and someone who’s not afraid to take on big business… and often wins… class action specialist Richard Spoor.

Gentlemen, Let’s debate…
4:54 Busi: Ian, let’s look at the potential harm. We’re talking about 48 airguns pumping or firing every ten seconds, over five months…

Ian: - I think you have to look at the real world and in the real world, this has been done for a very long period of time. There’s been numerous such surveys off the South African coast with no apparent damage… If you look at the science, look at what the scientists are saying, it’s speculative. They’re saying it may cause harm. No one is saying, it will cause harm. They don’t really know.

Busi: Richard - it’s based on speculation?

6:41 Richard: … Let’s also remember that this is step one in the process. Step two is the drilling through three kilometres of water deep, two kilometres into the rock, to extract oil and gas. It’s very technical, very complex and off the wild coast, it’s also extremely dangerous. The risk of oil spills, particularly along the coast is enormous. It’s manifest, it’s clear. I mean there’s nobody who can argue about it and what’s happening is that this risk is being assumed without consultation…

8:24 SIFISO: …Are we allowing a very dated consultation process to rule the legal frameworks in todays context? At the end of the day, we’ve got digital, we’ve got a whole lot of ways in which we can enhance the consultation process. We’ve seen it in a whole lot of ways in which this consultation process becomes the thing that holds back progress. We’ve seen it become the thing that takes these opportunities to court for five to ten years and companies walk away. We’ve seen it in many industries even outside this one as well.
… the first issue here is investor sentiment - that already is an indicator that it’s difficult to do business in SA. Over and above that, money follows value and at the end of tHe day, Shell will probably come back if the environment becomes conducive. But right now they have to weigh up and say if I have an equal opportunity for proven reserves or exploratory reserves between this country and that one…
12:01 BUSI - Richard is dying to jump in there
12:03 RICHARD: I want to be clear, if theres a problem in rolling out this grand vision for gas in South Africa, it’s not community consultation… the problem is governments policy and the onerous conditions they place.
17:06 RICHARD: It’s very simple - where I oart ways with Ian and Sifiso is Gwede Mantash and government have a grand plan, a grand scheme about the future for oil and gas in this country. They want to build a industry offshore, they want to transform our oceans for mining purposes not only oil and gas but the consultation that is not taking place is how is that going to affect our lives and how are we going to benefit . If you look at the west coast communities weve had a copper boom in the early days of the twentieth century, weve had a diamond boom that lasted fifty years hwta benefit have those communities derived? If fact nothing. If anything they’ve been degraded and harmed so now we come with this grand vision of oil and gas. Gwede has plans, they are pasing laws, they are amending the gas act, they are amending the MPRDA, talking about free rides and BEE and all kinds of clever schemes but we are the people who are going ot have this industry off-shore. We are going to face the consequences if there’s a spill and our fish stocks are destroyed. Talk to us about how we participate how we are going to benefit. How what you are going to be doing is going to affect us. It’s not a case for sandton and the stock exchange, it’s a case for the people who are physically on the ground. How is this massive industry that’s going to bring enormous wealth to this country, how is it going to impact on us and ow is it going to enhance on our lives. That’s the debate, that’s the consultation that needs to take place.
SIFISO: But you can’t over engineer develop right and so when you talk about a grand plan, youve got to figure out what’s a workable model that you can test, you develop, you scale. And so even in the consultation process, we can’t see the big picture always…

19:47 SIFISO - One of the things that Minister said is that if you don’;t know what sits on the other side, the legislation becomes quite onerous and what happens is that you try and overengineer something that you don’t actually know…

We seen that interms of the ways we’ve tested incentives in the country, infrastructure investment etc and it has worked for some of those projects.
20:40 RICHARD - Well, with respect, it’s simply not correct. Theres a hell of lot of engineering going on about governments free carry, what is our stake, what do we get out of it. There’s a big commitment about BEE, typically crony capitalists - what are they going to get out of it. They’re being tied into it. What’s the role for our state owned enterprises PETROSA we want stakes in this, we want stakes in that
RICHARD: our tax… but what you don’t see is what is in it for communities.

00:17 You don’t see that at all. So in terms of detailed engineering, there are layers and layers of complexity that have been generated but the main thing is how is this going to impact us, how are we going to benefit, that doesn’t form part of this planning at all.
00:27

Busi: Are the economic benefits then exaggerated then in this case? The potential economic benefits.

00:33 IAN: No i don’t think so because I think we are looking at prospecting, this is the beginning of the process. If you find gas in sufficient quantities which is a very big if, I have my doubts personally

00:44 RICHARD: That’s not true. There are very very substantial gas and oil resources - they are hard to tap, they are hard to get in, but they are substantial resources, there’s no question about it. The question is, should we be harnessing these resources, who will benefit. How are we participating and how is it going to change our country. To just say, look it’s speculative, might just happen, might not, so worry too much, is simply wrong.

01:12 IAN - I disagree with you, i disagree you.
RICHARD: There are massive resources.
IAN: I’m not aware, there’s been massive resources and if there was, we would’ve tapped into them long ago.


00:47 RICHARD: …We’ve got a history of dumping the cost on… a handful of people… not a handful… on poor black people and the benefits acrue to a smaller elite. And it’s that that is a fundamental problem. So, yes, we want to see growth and development. But as our West Coast clients say, “the diamonds passed us by, the copper passed us by, is oil gonna pass us by as well?”

01:33 We want to make sure that wherever development we undertake accrues to the advantage, not of a small group of crony capitalists and powerful elites, but that it accrues to the real benefit of ordinary South Africans, wherever they are.
01:21:28:05 - 01:21: 55:19 As is so often the case in our country, these debates are never simple. What’s clear is that this is about MORE than just choosing between whales on one side or natural gas on the other. It’s about understanding that siding with either one, has significant consequences.

This meant that South Africa would potentially lose out on massive development and employment opportunities, he added. This background brings us to the heart of the debate. For the moment Shell have been ordered to put an end to its seismic surveys but should this this mean the end of gas exploration in the country as some environmentalists believe? Not so fast it seems! In the West Coast, Searcher GeoData, which provides subsurface exploration data, has been awarded a reconnaissance permit for a multi-client speculative 2D and/or 3D marine seismic programme to explore for oil and gas over vast areas of the ocean stretching from Cape Point to the Namibian border in an area known as the Orange Basin. Its environmental management plan states the programme will potentially allow South Africa to “optimise its own indigenous resources to provide its identified oil and gas needs, rather than having to import, as at present”. Are we placing the real needs of employment and economic growth in places like the Eastern Cape above the protection of the environment? And does science support the notion that seismic surveys will destroy the coastline? Is it one or the other, or can it be both? And if seismic surveys are here to stay, how then do we still protect the environment? Let's debate!
